questions.question: Profits inside a Stocks & Shares ISA are…
questions.explanation: Gains and dividends inside an ISA are tax-free.

questions.question: Which of these is generally lower risk?
questions.explanation: A global index fund spreads your money across thousands of companies.

questions.question: A trading app gives you a free share. Before you sell it, check…
options: Any minimum holding period in the terms
questions.explanation: Many free-share offers require you to keep the share, or the account, for a set time.

questions.question: Using the Rule of 72, at 6% a year, roughly how long does money take to double?
Fund A charges 1.5% a year, Fund B 0.2%. On £10,000, how much more does A cost per year?
questions.explanation: 1.3% of £10,000 = £130 a year, and the gap compounds over time.

questions.question: £2,000 grows by 7% a year, compounded yearly. Roughly how much after 10 years?
questions.explanation: £2,000 × 1.07¹⁰ ≈ £3,934. Simple interest would only give £3,400.

questions.question: Diversification means…
options: Putting everything in one hot stock
questions.explanation: Spreading your money means one bad pick can't sink you.

questions.question: An index fund aims to…
options: Beat the market by picking winners
Track a market index like the FTSE 100
questions.explanation: Index funds track a market rather than trying to beat it, which usually keeps fees low.

questions.question: Why do long-term investors often sit tight through short-term drops?
options: Markets have historically recovered over long periods, though nothing is guaranteed
questions.explanation: History favours patience, but past performance isn't a guarantee.

questions.question: “Investments can go down as well as up” means…
options: You could get back less than you put in
questions.explanation: Investing carries the risk of losing money.

questions.question: A dividend is…
options: Part of a company's profits paid to shareholders
questions.explanation: Companies may share profits with shareholders as dividends.

questions.question: Pound-cost averaging means…
options: Investing a fixed amount regularly, buying more when prices are low
questions.explanation: Regular investing smooths out the price you pay.

questions.question: Your fund rises 10%, then falls 10%. Overall you are…
Is crypto held on an exchange covered by the FSCS?
questions.explanation: Crypto isn't FSCS protected. If an exchange fails, you could lose everything.

questions.question: Who regulates most UK investment firms?
questions.explanation: The Financial Conduct Authority regulates investment firms. Check the FCA Register before investing.

questions.question: A platform charges 0.45% a year. On £20,000, that's…
An investment promising “guaranteed 20% a month” is…
questions.explanation: Guaranteed high returns are the classic scam promise.

questions.question: A Stocks & Shares ISA protects you from…
questions.explanation: An ISA is a tax wrapper. Your investments can still fall.

questions.question: Your investments grow 6% in a year when inflation is 4%. Your real return is roughly…
questions.explanation: Real return ≈ 6% − 4% = 2%.

questions.question: Before investing, many guides suggest you first…
options: Build an emergency fund and clear expensive debt
questions.explanation: Expensive debt usually costs more than investments earn, and a buffer stops you selling at a bad time.

questions.question: Buying a share means:
options: Owning a small part of a company
questions.explanation: Shares are ownership stakes; their value moves with the company and market.

questions.question: An index fund invests in:
options: All the companies in an index, like the FTSE 100 or S&P 500, in one fund
questions.explanation: Index funds track a whole market slice, giving instant diversification at low cost.

questions.question: Which type of fund usually has the lowest ongoing fees?
questions.explanation: Trackers just follow an index, so running costs are far lower than active management.

questions.question: The ongoing charges figure (OCF) of a fund:
options: Is the yearly fee deducted from your investment, and small differences compound hugely
questions.explanation: A 1% fee vs 0.1% fee can cost tens of thousands over a lifetime of investing.

questions.question: Compound growth in investing works best with:
options: Time: leaving investments to grow over years or decades
questions.explanation: Compounding needs time; most of the growth in long investing careers comes from reinvested returns.

questions.question: 'Time in the market beats timing the market' means:
options: Staying invested long-term usually beats trying to predict the perfect moment
questions.explanation: Missing the market's best days by sitting out can badly damage long-term returns.

questions.question: Volatility in investments is:
options: Normal: prices move up and down in the short term while long-term growth is uneven
questions.explanation: Dips are part of investing; panic-selling during them locks in losses.

questions.question: Diversification reduces risk because:
options: Losses in one holding can be offset by others, so you're not betting everything on one outcome
questions.explanation: Diversification manages risk; it doesn't eliminate it.

questions.question: Money lost when a stock's price falls:
options: Is not covered by the FSCS; the FSCS protects you if the firm fails, not from market losses
questions.explanation: FSCS covers firm failure up to limits, not investment losses; this is a key difference from cash savings.

questions.question: Cryptocurrency investments:
options: Are generally not FSCS protected and can fall to zero
Are guaranteed by the Bank of England
questions.explanation: Crypto is high risk, largely unregulated for consumer protection, and you can lose everything.

questions.question: A celebrity promotes a coin or investment scheme online. This usually suggests:
options: A high-risk or scam promotion; celebrities are paid and schemes like this are a classic red flag
questions.explanation: Endorsed schemes are a well-known scam pattern; assume risk until independently verified.

questions.question: 'Pound-cost averaging' means:
options: Investing a fixed amount regularly, so you buy more shares when prices are low
questions.explanation: Regular investing smooths your entry price and removes the temptation to time the market.

questions.question: Before investing, which should be done first?
options: Pay off high-interest debt and build an emergency fund
questions.explanation: Clearing debt that costs 20%+ beats most investment returns, and the buffer stops forced selling.

questions.question: Stocks & Shares ISA tax treatment means:
options: You pay no tax on gains or dividends within the ISA, within the annual allowance
You get a refund on losses
questions.explanation: The ISA wrapper shelters gains and income up to the annual allowance.

questions.question: A SIPP is:
options: A personal pension you control, giving tax relief on contributions
questions.explanation: SIPPs attract tax relief on contributions and lock money until pension age.

questions.question: 'Representative' investment returns shown in adverts are:
options: Often past performance, which is not a reliable indicator of future results
questions.explanation: Past performance is a warning label, not a promise; adverts must say so for a reason.

questions.question: Higher-risk asset classes like emerging markets typically offer:
options: Potentially higher returns with much bigger swings and losses
questions.explanation: Risk and potential return travel together; higher reward means higher possible loss.

questions.question: Dividends are:
options: Payments some companies make to shareholders from profits
questions.explanation: Dividend-paying shares give income; within an ISA this income is tax-free.

questions.question: Bonds generally are:
options: Lower risk than shares, paying interest, but can still lose value if sold early or the issuer defaults
questions.explanation: Bonds sit lower on the risk ladder than shares but are not risk-free.

questions.question: Reinvesting dividends instead of taking them as cash:
options: Feeds compounding and can substantially increase final value over decades
questions.explanation: Reinvestment is compounding in action.

questions.question: An investment platform's fee structure matters because:
options: High platform fees compound against you just like fund fees do
questions.explanation: Compare platform fees, fund fees and dealing charges together, not just fund costs.

questions.question: 'Fractional shares' let you:
options: Buy part of a share, so expensive shares become accessible
questions.explanation: Fractional investing lowers the entry barrier, useful for regular small amounts.

questions.question: 'Free share' sign-up offers usually require:
options: You to open an account, sometimes deposit or trade first; read the terms before assuming it's free
A credit check that damages your score always
questions.explanation: The shares are often conditional on deposits or trades; worth it only if you'd use the platform anyway.

questions.question: An investment that guarantees a high fixed return with no risk is:
options: Almost certainly a scam; genuinely risky-free high returns don't exist
questions.explanation: Guaranteed high returns with no risk is the textbook scam pitch.

questions.question: The FCA Register is used to:
options: Check that a firm or person is authorised to give financial services in the UK
questions.explanation: Before investing with anyone, check them on the FCA Register; unauthorised firms can't be compensated.

questions.question: A fund that tracks the FTSE 100 holds:
options: Shares in the 100 largest UK-listed companies by size
questions.explanation: Index composition is public; trackers simply hold it.

questions.question: Selling investments during a crash typically:
options: Turns a paper loss into a real one and misses the recovery
questions.explanation: Long-term investing means enduring downturns; selling at the bottom is the classic expensive mistake.

questions.question: Investment fees of 2% per year versus 0.2% over 30 years can differ by:
options: Tens of thousands of pounds on a modest portfolio
questions.explanation: Fee drag compounds just like returns do, in reverse.

questions.question: Which is generally the most tax-efficient home for long-term investments in the UK?
options: A Stocks & Shares ISA (up to the allowance)
questions.explanation: ISA wrappers shield investment growth from tax up to the annual allowance.

questions.question: 'Ponzi scheme' red flags include:
options: Consistent 'guaranteed' returns paid from new investors' money, and pressure to recruit others
Being listed on a stock exchange
questions.explanation: If returns depend on recruitment or feel too smooth to be real, walk away.
